chapter_name: Treatment Settings, Health Care System, and Outcome
chapter_title: Treatment Settings, Health Care System, and Outcome

questions.question_text: All of the following statements regarding wraparound services are accurate except:

options.text: Wraparound services are community based.
Wraparound services are child and family centered.
A problem is identified based on a deficit model and ameliorating the problem is the treatment focus.
Value is placed on cultural competency.
The family determines the mix of services.

correct_answer.text: A problem is identified based on a deficit model and ameliorating the problem is the treatment focus.

correct_answers.text: A problem is identified based on a deficit model and ameliorating the problem is the treatment focus.

questions.explanation: In contrast to the traditional mental health treatment that uses a deficit model, wraparound services use strength based approaches that uncover positive coping mechanisms and resiliency factors in the family. Wraparound services are especially beneficial to the children and families that have significant emotional and behavioral difficulties and previously experienced treatment failure. They are child and family centered, community and strength based, and contain culturally competent services that integrate the family as an active participant in building the treatment plan. (Ref. 1, pp. 926-927; Ref. 2. p. 331)

questions.question_text: Research shows which of the following groups of youth are most likely to respond to multisystemic therapy?

options.text: Youth with bipolar disorders
Youth who are juvenile offenders
Youth who are psychotic
Youth with depressions
Youth with anxiety disorders

questions.explanation: Youth who are juvenile offenders and youth who are abusing substances and are at risk for out-of-home placement respond to the MST more robustly. Short-term data support the efficacy of reducing inpatient psychiatric hospitalization and out-of-home placements, improving externalizing symptoms and family relationships, and increasing school attendance. (Ref. 1, pp. 932-933)

questions.question_text: The federal government established the Child and Adolescent Service System Program (CASSP) in 1984. All of the following are major principles of the CASSP except:

options.text: To coordinate and collaborate among different agencies and to integrate services across agencies
To serve youth in more restrictive and structured environments or settings to meet their clinical needs
To individualize care that recognizes strengths in the child, family, and community
To provide culturally competent services
To include the family at every level of the clinical process and system organization

correct_answer.text: To serve youth in more restrictive and structured environments or settings to meet their clinical needs

correct_answers.text: To serve youth in more restrictive and structured environments or settings to meet their clinical needs

questions.explanation: One of the five principles of CASSP is to serve youth in the communities or in the least restrictive environment or setting to meet their clinical needs. (Ref. 1, pp. 926-927; N. C. Winters and W. P. Metz: The Wraparound Approach in System of Care. Pscyhiatr Clin N Am, 32: 132-151, 2009)

questions.question_text: According to the article "Physician Leadership in Residential Treatment for Children and Adolescents" by Christopher Bellonci (2010), all of the following statements are accurate except:

options.text: Residential treatment centers (RTCs) formally require a physician to be the medical director who can provide the leadership.
Integrating and incorporating all the past and current data, the physician needs to lead the team to make diagnoses and to develop treatment plans.
The physician can provide a comprehensive review of the child's and family's strengths and needs.
The physician also plays a role in teaching child care staff theories regarding development and mental illness and its treatments.

Past treatment histories and records and current information about the child need to be collected, and the physician needs to interpret the data and to work with the multidisciplinary team to develop a bio-psycho-social-educational formulation.

correct_answer.text: Residential treatment centers (RTCs) formally require a physician to be the medical director who can provide the leadership.

correct_answers.text: Residential treatment centers (RTCs) formally require a physician to be the medical director who can provide the leadership.

questions.explanation: Even though physicians are increasingly included in leadership roles in RTCs, licensing for most RTCs does not formally request a medical director. Traditionally, physicians/ psychiatrists are responsible for prescribing psychotropic medications without further integration into the administrative or leadership structure. (C. Bellonci: Physician Leadership in Residential Treatment for Children and Adolescents. Child Adolesc Psychiatric Clin N Am, 19: 21-30, 2010)

questions.question_text: All of the following statements accurately describe the Intensive In-Home Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Service (IICAPS) developed at Yale in 1997 except:

options.text: The IICAPS believes that the family has the capacity and is essential to make sustainable changes in a child's life.
A psychologist is required to serve as the director to co-lead the interdisciplinary team meetings.
The IICAPS serves children and adolescents with serious emotional and behavioral problems in home/family settings.
The families have to be partners in the treatment process and co-lead the treatment planning.
The IICAPS provides 24/7 mobile crisis services.

correct_answer.text: A psychologist is required to serve as the director to co-lead the interdisciplinary team meetings.

correct_answers.text: A psychologist is required to serve as the director to co-lead the interdisciplinary team meetings.

questions.explanation: IICAPS requires a child and adolescent psychiatrist to serve as the medical director to co-lead the interdisciplinary treatment rounds. Programmatically, IICAPS is designed as the following: six to eight cases per team, four teams to a rounds group, one to four rounds groups to a program, and 15 programs to a network. (Ref. 1, p. 933)

questions.question_text: All of the following statements regarding milieu treatment (MT) are accurate except:

options.text: Most outcome studies have used "change analysis" (i.e., the differences between before and after service delivery).
Conclusive evidence has demonstrated the effectiveness of MT.
Therapeutic milieu is central to inpatient hospital units (IU), partial hospital (PH), day treatment (DT), and residential treatment centers (RTCs).
Managed care involvement has not lessened the difficulty of accessing and appropriately using IU care across the nation.
IU, PH, DT, and RTCs are considered as restrictive or intensive services, but federal reports combine IU and RTCs into statistical analysis, and PH and DT are now grouped into outpatient treatments.

correct_answer.text: Conclusive evidence has demonstrated the effectiveness of MT.

correct_answers.text: Conclusive evidence has demonstrated the effectiveness of MT.

questions.explanation: Because of the significant difficulties in study design and implementation, even though some studies have shown positive outcomes of RTCs and IU services, conclusive evidence demonstrating MT's effectiveness is still largely lacking.. (Ref. 1, pp. 939-940)

questions.question_text: All of the following critical factors should be determined prior to admission to MT except:

options.text: None of the above
Contact with delinquent peers for those with disruptive disorders
Child and family functioning
Consistency of discipline within the family
Family perceived stress

questions.explanation: None of the listed factors should be excluded as critical factors that should be determined prior to admission, and another factor is extent of drug and/or alcohol use or abuse. (Ref. 1 p. 941)

questions.question_text: If a child is at high risk of danger to self or others, which of the following MT programs is not appropriate?

options.text: Day treatment
Partial hospital
Residential treatment center
All of the above
Acute inpatient

questions.explanation: A residential treatment center would not be sufficient to provide care for youth at high risk of danger to self or others. Acute inpatient is the most appropriate setting, and partial hospital and day treatment can potentially provide the needed acute services. For those with low risk of danger to self or others, acute inpatient is the least appropriate, but PH, DT, and RTCs all can provide the appropriate level of care. (Ref. 1. p. 942; Ref. 2, p. 332)

questions.question_text: Based on the most recent research findings, all of the following statements regarding aggressive behaviors, seclusion, and restraint in MT settings are correct except:

options.text: Some case studies have shown how leadership serves to decrease seclusion and restraint through organizational and cultural change.
Stricter federal policy on seclusion and restraint is associated with the highly publicized concerns of the adverse effects of mechanical and other forms of restraint.
A recent study shows hospitalized youth prefer timeout to medication (e.g., chemical restraint and prn medication).
Multiple attempts have been made to reduce seclusion and restraint.
All MT programs are expected to be able to manage youth with highly aggressive, violent, and destructive behaviors.

correct_answer.text: A recent study shows hospitalized youth prefer timeout to medication (e.g., chemical restraint and prn medication).

correct_answers.text: A recent study shows hospitalized youth prefer timeout to medication (e.g., chemical restraint and prn medication).

questions.explanation: A recent study shows hospitalized youth prefer medication to timeout or seclusion in contrast to earlier studies advocating for timeout. (Ref. 1, pp. 941-943)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best way to prevent elopement from MT programs?

options.text: Effective communication among staff and between staff and patients
Negative consequences such as timeout, seclusion, and restraint
Sufficient dosage of psychotropic medications
Onsite schooling
Use of video surveillance system

correct_answer.text: Effective communication among staff and between staff and patients

correct_answers.text: Effective communication among staff and between staff and patients

questions.explanation: Effective communication among staff and between staff and patients is the best way to prevent elopement and other risky behaviors in the MT programs. (Ref. 1, p. 943)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is (are) the risk factor(s) warranting an admission to an appropriate MT program?

options.text: A suicide attempter with clear abnormal mental state, or an individual with suicidal ideation
All of the above
Lack of adequate supervision or support outside of therapeutic milieu
An individual with persistent wish to die
Unsafe to return home because of unresolved biopsychosocial risk factors that are unlikely to change

questions.explanation: All listed are the risk factors that warrant an admission to an appropriate MT program. (Ref. 1. p. 943)

questions.question_text: All of the following safety factors should be considered prior to discharging youth from an MT program to a lower level of care except:

options.text: Family-related issues addressed
Suicidal potential is minimal
Crisis issue resolved to acceptable level
Home environment is sanitized (e.g., no firearms and medication secured)
None of the above

questions.explanation: None of the listed safety factors should be excluded when considering discharging youth from an MT program to a lower level of care. Other safety factors may include aftercare planning such as providing appropriate psychoeducation to the family and patient and setting up realistic transition plans (ongoing psychosocial interventions and medication follow ups). (Ref. 1, p. 943)

questions.question_text: All of the following are recommended to assure effective milieu treatment except:

options.text: Discharge only when a lower level of care can provide sufficient services
Actively involve the family
Require onsite school education
Optimize safety for patients, peers, and staff members
Actively address the factors identified in the formulation and treatment plan

questions.explanation: Onsite school education may not be available to all the MT programs and is a key factor for assuring effective milieu treatment. Providing financial support for duration of needed treatment is also recommended. (Ref. 1, p. 944)

questions.question_text: All of the following correctly describe the differences between residential treatment centers (RTCs) and inpatient hospital units (IU) except:

options.text: Youth view themselves as "residents" in RTCs in contrast to "sick persons" in IUs.
African American youth are less likely to be admitted to RTCS.
RTCs expect less regression than IUs.
RTCs provide more comprehensive services than inpatient hospital units.
Only IU provides 24-hour nursing and medical care.

correct_answer.text: African American youth are less likely to be admitted to RTCS.

correct_answers.text: African American youth are less likely to be admitted to RTCS.

questions.explanation: African American youth are more likely to be admitted to RTCs than whites. Data also shows that mental health services are disproportionally provided to white youth in juvenile justice facilities compared to those of minority races. (Ref. 1. pp. 945-946)

questions.question_text: All of the following factors predict poor treatment outcome for RTCs except:

options.text: Below-average level of intelligence
Presence of psychosis
Inadequate aftercare services
Longer length of stay
Presence of antisocial and bizarre behavior

questions.explanation: Inadequate length of stay and insufficient duration to allow for consolidation of gains from the treatment predicts poor outcome. Another negative outcome factor is a dysfunctional family. (Ref. 1, p. 946)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the main tool that is used for assessing RTCs' treatment outcome?

options.text: Child Symptom Inventory (CSI)
Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL)
Child Functional Assessment Rating Scales (CFARS)
Children's Global Assessment Scale (CGAS)
Behavior Assessment System for Children, Second Edition (BASC-2)

questions.explanation: Child Functional Assessment Rating Scales (CFARS) is the main tool that is used to evaluate residential treatment outcomes. Using this tool, administrators and providers can generate data through a system-wide assessment and report the findings efficiently via a Web-based system. (Ref. 1.  . 946)

questions.question_text: All of the following are considered common functions of an acute inpatient psychiatric unit (IU) except:

options.text: Stabilizing symptoms and crisis
Minimizing potential for harm (e.g., separation from family and community and monitoring behavior)
Developing a treatment plan and rapidly implementing it
Case formulation and diagnosis
Psychological testing

questions.explanation: Psychological testing is not a common function of an acute psychiatric inpatient unit. Disposition planning and transition to less restrictive care are other common functions of an IU.. (Ref. 1. p. 947)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is associated with higher readmission rates after discharge from an IU?

options.text: Harsh parental discipline
Disengaged parent-child relations
All of the above
None of the above
Severe conduct problems

questions.explanation: A 2004 study by J. C. Blader indicates that predictors for the readmission of 109 school-aged children who were previously hospitalized in a psychiatric facility are severe conduct problems, disengaged parent-child relations, and harsh parental discipline. (Ref. 1, p. 948)

questions.question_text: All of the following statements regarding partial hospitalization (PH) and day treatment (DT) are accurate except:

options.text: Both PH and DT must be part of a hospital clinic or an IU.
Both PH and DT are less than 24-hour hospital-level daily care to prevent relapses and rehospitalizations.
The PH model can be employed in specialized milieu treatments for substance-related disorders, eating disorders, victims of abuse, and those with medical and psychiatric comorbidities.
Chemical or manual restraints are not commonly used in DT.
Youth in the programs are expected to have sufficient self-control to avert dangerous behavior.

correct_answer.text: Both PH and DT must be part of a hospital clinic or an IU.

correct_answers.text: Both PH and DT must be part of a hospital clinic or an IU.

questions.explanation: Unlike PH, DT can be freestanding or a part of an IU, a hospital clinic, a school, or an RTC. DTs are structured and attend to patients' educational needs and provide multimodel treatments. The restrictive practice (i.e., seclusion and restraints) in DTs is limited to those methods acceptable and available in most school or home environments, whereas the restrictive practice in PH depends on the hospital configuration. Chemical or physical restraints are not used in DT programs, but personal ("therapeutic") holding of young children and quiet rooms are sometimes used in certain DT programs. (Ref. 1, p. 949)

questions.question_text: All of the following are considered as routine laboratory tests prior to or upon admission to a psychiatric facility except:

options.text: Electroencephalography (EEG)
Complete blood counts
Thyroid function tests
Liver functioning tests
Pregnancy tests for female patients of child-bearing potential

questions.explanation: Electroencephalography (EEG) is not a routine test, but can be potentially useful in cases of suspected seizure disorders such as Landau-Kleffner syndrome (manifesting as declination of language skills). Neuroimaging studies are not considered as routine laboratory tests, but at times can be useful to rule out an alternative etiology of psychosis (such as tumors, hemorrhage, and other brain lesions, etc.). Blood levels of certain psychotropic medications may be useful, and toxicological analysis of urine is a common routine admission test. (Ref. 3, p. 873)
